subject: Prospective PhD student (Fall 2027): what people think can be inferred from what they share
body:
Dear Prof. Li,

I'm Morgan Reyes, an M.S. Data Science student at Lakeshore University, graduating in December 2026. I'm applying to the Khoury HCI PhD program for Fall 2027 and would like to work with you in the PEACH Lab.

My interest started with a research project on bus ridership. While building features from a mobility dataset described as anonymized, I combined two columns that were each supposedly anonymous: where riders first boarded each day, and where their phones spent the night. Together they put many people on a few blocks. I dropped the feature, but the experience stayed with me. I keep wondering what people think can be figured out from what they share, with apps and now with AI tools, and whether they could ever actually see it.

That's why your lab's work stands out to me. Your CHI 2024 study found that users' wrong mental models kept them from seeing the risks of what they disclose to chatbots. Your position paper with Niloofar Mireshghallah argues that inference and aggregation get far less attention than memorization. Together they describe the gap I want to study. In a course usability study of an AutoML tool, I also saw the same thing from the analyst side: participants assumed the tool already knew which columns were sensitive.

Are you planning to take new PhD students for Fall 2027? I'd be glad to talk if you have time.

Best regards,
Morgan Reyes
M.S. Data Science, Lakeshore University
morgan.reyes@example.edu
